name: LangRelay – AI Translation & Multilingual
author: langrelay

sections.description:
LangRelay is a WordPress translation plugin that makes your site multilingual. AI translates your pages, posts and products. Each translation goes live as you choose in the LangRelay Dashboard, and your site serves it at its own address, with hreflang tags and a language switcher handled automatically.

Most translation plugins stop at the words on the page. LangRelay also translates your meta titles and descriptions and gives every translated page its own address, so your site gets found in every market you sell in.

What you get

  • AI translations, live as you choose. Machine translation drafts each page; it goes live once ready (the default), after a hold, or only once you approve it. Free checks hold a page with untranslated text, the wrong language or a changed price; legal pages, pricing pages and sweeping changes always wait for you.
  • An address for every language. Each translated page lives under its language prefix, like yoursite.com/nl/about-us, and you can give it an address in that language, like yoursite.com/nl/over-ons, in the LangRelay Dashboard.
  • Automatic hreflang and SEO metadata. Hreflang and canonical tags on every translated page with no manual setup, and translated meta titles, descriptions and social text (details below).
  • Language switcher. A menu or list with flags and language names, in one of four styles. A plain list of links is rendered with the page, so visitors without JavaScript and search engines still see every language. Add it as a Gutenberg block, Elementor widget, shortcode, HTML snippet or menu items, or float it in the corner you choose.
  • WooCommerce pages. Product and shop pages translate like any other page once their translation is live.
  • Visitors offered their language. A visitor who reads one of your languages is offered the page in it or, if you choose, taken there on arrival. Set it in the LangRelay Dashboard.

Why a multilingual WordPress site matters

  • English is only 16% of the internet. The other 84% is your addressable market.
  • Google ranks translated pages separately. A multilingual site can multiply your organic traffic without adding new content.
  • AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini) increasingly answer in the user’s native language. Without translated pages, you don’t show up.

How it works

  1. Install the plugin, go to Settings > LangRelay and click Connect to LangRelay. Sign in to LangRelay or create your account there, approve the connection in the LangRelay Dashboard, and you’re back on your site, connected.
  2. In the LangRelay Dashboard, pick your languages.
  3. Approve your first page there; after it, pages follow your setting. Once a translation is live, your site serves it at its own address, with the language switcher, hreflang and canonical tags taken care of.

No content duplication, no manual translation interface, no separate posts to manage.

Multilingual SEO done right

LangRelay handles the SEO work that usually takes hours per language:

  • hreflang and x-default tags on every translated page and its original
  • A canonical tag on every translated page naming its own address in that language. When your SEO plugin points a page’s canonical at another page of your site, the translation points at that page in the same language once it is live; a canonical to another website is left as it is
  • An address of its own for each language version, under its language prefix, with the page’s lang (and dir="rtl" for a right-to-left language)
  • Translated meta titles, descriptions, and Open Graph and Twitter text in your page’s HTML, whichever plugin writes them
  • og:url, og:locale, an og:locale:alternate for each other language the page is live in, and twitter:url, naming the translated page’s own address and language
  • Your translated pages in the sitemaps of Yoast SEO, Rank Math, All in One SEO, SEOPress, The SEO Framework and XML Sitemap Generator for Google, each with all its language versions
  • A sitemap of your translated pages when your site uses WordPress’s own sitemap or no sitemap plugin

Search engines understand which language to serve to which visitor.

What makes LangRelay different

Your site serves exactly the translation LangRelay recorded as live.

The same sentence is translated once and reused wherever it appears, even on 500 pages, like a line in your footer.

Pricing

Plans and prices are at langrelay.com/pricing.

Meet Relay

Relay is the AI assistant in the LangRelay Dashboard. Ask it about your Site, and it can start machine translation for a page, fetch a page again after you change it, or suggest a better translation for a sentence you select. It never approves a translation itself.

External services

LangRelay’s Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Data Processing Agreement are at langrelay.com. By using this plugin you agree to LangRelay’s Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

LangRelay API, from your site

Your site calls the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) over HTTPS, always with this site’s connection credential. It never sends your page content.

What is sent: when you connect, the one-time connection code. On connecting and in an hourly health check: your site’s address, WordPress and plugin versions and an installation ID. The health check also says whether WooCommerce is installed and active, and its version and, while it is active, the addresses of your store’s published cart, checkout and account pages; which of Yoast SEO, Rank Math, All in One SEO, SEOPress, The SEO Framework or XML Sitemap Generator for Google makes your sitemap, and its version (or that WordPress’s own sitemap, or none, does); and whether your site has its own robots.txt. No other plugin is named. About a minute after you save content: the address of each published page you saved, or that a menu, category, tag, site title, tagline or theme changed, with the time and installation ID. Within ten minutes of an update to WordPress, an active plugin or your theme: its name and old and new versions. Within ten minutes of a translated page being shown in its original language because your page layout changed (each page at most once every six hours): which page and language, and how much of the translation still fitted. When you erase a customer’s personal data: their profile key (see revenue below), again later if LangRelay could not be reached.
What is received: your site’s languages and your pages’ approved translations, which the plugin caches on your site. It checks them hourly with the health check, and on visitor page requests at most once per refresh interval (one minute by default) or when an approved translation changes. Only when an administrator opens Settings > LangRelay, at most every five minutes (or a minute later when LangRelay could not be reached): your LangRelay plan, this month’s word usage and welcome grant, the pages waiting to be translated (titles and addresses) and the plan that would translate them now, with its price and a link to the LangRelay Dashboard. Only while that screen is open and in view, at most every half minute (it asks every twenty seconds and stops after twenty minutes; a minute later when LangRelay could not be reached): how far your first translation has come (the language, how many texts are translated, whether the page is live and checked), the live page’s address and a link to your Site in the LangRelay Dashboard.

LangRelay API, from your visitors’ browsers

A small script that ships with this plugin, served from your site and never from LangRelay, calls the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) from the visitor’s browser: on every page while your Site counts page views; otherwise on pages with the language switcher, on translated pages and, while Visitor language is on, on every page that has a translation. It follows your Site’s Dynamic content setting in LangRelay, on by default.

Translations: when a visitor opens a page, unless their browser has a fresh copy, it reads your site’s languages and, on a translated page, the approved, live translations in that language it needs for text that appears after the page loads (such as a mini-cart) and the addresses of your translated pages. It sends your site’s public key (printed in the page, not a password) and, on a translated page, its language and which part of your translations it needs (a version and a part number).
Page views, for your Site’s visitor analytics: once for each page a visitor opens, it sends your site’s public key; the page’s address without any query string; the visitor’s language as your site names it; whether the page was shown translated, could have been, or was read in the original language; and, when another website’s link brought the visitor, that website’s domain name only. Never the page’s text or title, any cookie, the full address of the page the visitor came from, or any identifier, except the profile key of a customer signed in to your shop while revenue tracking is on. Nothing is received. From it LangRelay works out the visitor’s country, kind of device, browser and operating system, and a visitor code that changes every day, so a visitor cannot be recognised from one day to the next (a signed-in customer’s profile key is the one exception); the IP address and browser details are used only for that and never stored. Counting stores nothing on the visitor’s device. Page views are kept for three months, then only totals. None is sent when the browser has Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track on, or for people signed in with a role left out under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced (administrators and editors by default). Counting is on by default: switch off Visitor analytics under your Site’s Settings → Analytics in the LangRelay Dashboard, and it stops within about a minute. LangRelay’s Privacy Policy and Data Processing Agreement describe how this data is handled.

Visitor language, in your visitors’ browsers

Suggesting or redirecting to a visitor’s language sends nothing to anyone. It stores the visitor’s choice and a redirect marker in their browser (localStorage, sessionStorage, no cookie; details in the FAQ).

WordPress’s own translations, from WordPress.org

Translated pages use the official translations of WordPress, your theme and plugins installed on your site. Once a day at most per language, WordPress’s own installer downloads those of WordPress, WooCommerce and your theme that a language lacks (on your click, your plugins’ too), from WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org, downloads.wordpress.org); turn this off under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced. It sends what WordPress sends when it checks for updates: your WordPress version, your site’s languages and the versions of your active plugins and theme. Nothing goes to LangRelay. The WordPress.org Privacy Policy applies.

The “Powered by LangRelay” link

The language switcher’s menu and the language suggestion show a “Powered by LangRelay” link to langrelay.com, on by default (a paid plan can turn it off in the LangRelay Dashboard). Only when a visitor clicks it does langrelay.com open in a new tab, with your site’s domain name, whether the link was in the switcher or the suggestion, and your site’s public key in its address, so LangRelay can tell which site the visit came from. The page the visitor was on is not sent.

LangRelay API, for your shop’s revenue (WooCommerce)

When WooCommerce is active and you switch on revenue tracking (off by default) under your Site’s Settings → Analytics in the LangRelay Dashboard, your site’s server, never the shopper’s browser, tells the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) what happens to its orders, so the Dashboard can show your revenue and the language each order came from. Nothing is sent while it is off.

What is sent, about a minute after an order is placed at checkout, paid, refunded or cancelled, in batches and again later if LangRelay could not be reached: the order’s ID, what happened, the amount (the order’s total, or the refund’s) with its currency, when it happened, and the language the shopper browsed in (the checkout page’s, or else that of the page they last added a product from, which WooCommerce keeps in the shopper’s existing cart session; no new cookie); a signed-in customer’s profile key (below); this site’s connection credential and installation ID. For an order placed at checkout, also the shopper’s IP address and browser details as WooCommerce recorded them, which LangRelay turns into that day’s visitor code and never stores. Never the shopper’s name, email address, postal address, phone number, customer account or what they bought. What is received: whether each order event was recorded. Orders are kept while your Site exists; an order’s visitor code is removed 90 days after the order. Switching revenue tracking off stops the sending within about a minute and drops what was not sent yet.

Customers signed in to your shop: while revenue tracking is on, each gets a pseudonymous profile key, so the Dashboard can show which pages your customers came in on before they ordered. Your site’s server computes it from their account number in your shop and a secret LangRelay hands it, never from an email address, and it does not name them. It is printed in the pages they view, sent with their page views and orders, and links their visits across days. Never for guests, for people signed in with a role left out under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced, or, when the WP Consent API plugin is installed, for a visitor who has not consented to statistics. LangRelay keeps it on page views for three months and on orders for as long as the order. When you erase a customer’s personal data under Tools > Erase Personal Data, the plugin asks LangRelay to remove their key from their orders and never computes one for them again. LangRelay receives no name, email address or customer number with it.

LangRelay Dashboard

Only when you click Connect to LangRelay does your browser go to the LangRelay Dashboard (app.langrelay.com) to approve the connection and back, with your site’s address, installation ID, WordPress site language, title (which names your LangRelay organization) and the address to return to in the address your browser opens.

Only when you click Upgrade in the Dashboard on Settings > LangRelay does the LangRelay Dashboard’s plan page open in a new tab, at the address LangRelay gave, with your organization’s ID and the suggested plan in that address. The plugin never changes your plan; you upgrade in the Dashboard.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the langrelay folder to /wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate through Plugins in WordPress.
  3. Go to Settings > LangRelay and click Connect to LangRelay. Sign in to LangRelay, or create your account right there, approve the connection in the LangRelay Dashboard, and you’re returned to your site, connected.
  4. Pick your languages in the LangRelay Dashboard and approve your first page. After it, pages go live as your publishing setting says (by default, as soon as each is ready). Your site starts serving each one within about a minute of going live. With W3 Total Cache, WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, WP Super Cache, WP Fastest Cache, Cache Enabler, SiteGround Optimizer, Nginx Helper, Breeze or SpinupWP, a changed translation also leaves the page cache within a minute or two; a server-level cache without one of these plugins can hold the previous version until it expires.

There’s nothing else to set up: approving the connection binds your installation to a Site in the LangRelay Dashboard, and your languages are chosen there.

Can’t be redirected back to your site (staging, localhost)? Paste a connection code from the Dashboard instead, under Connect manually with a code on the Settings > LangRelay page.
sections.faq:
What does this plugin do?

It makes your WordPress site multilingual. AI translates your pages, each translation goes live as you choose in the LangRelay Dashboard, and your site serves each one at its own address, with hreflang tags and a language switcher. You don’t manage translated posts manually.

How is this different from other translation plugins?

Two big things. First, you choose how translations go live: as soon as they are ready (the default), after a hold, or only once you approve them. Free checks hold a page with untranslated text, the wrong language or a changed price, legal pages, pricing pages and sweeping changes always wait for you, and your site serves exactly the translation LangRelay recorded as live. Second, a sentence that appears across your whole site is translated once and reused, not once per page.

Switching from another translation plugin?

Coming from a service like Weglot, or a manual translation plugin like WPML or Polylang? Two things change:

  • You stop maintaining translations by hand. No duplicate posts or separate editors to keep in sync. LangRelay applies approved translations to your pages as they are served, so your content lives in one place.
  • You choose how pages go live. Right away, after a hold, or only once you approve them, as you set in the LangRelay Dashboard; your site serves exactly the translation LangRelay recorded as live.

Keep your content and keep your domain.

Which languages are supported?

The LangRelay Dashboard currently offers Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, and Turkish, both as the language your site is written in and as languages to translate into.

Do I need a LangRelay account?

Yes. LangRelay is a cloud service. If you don’t have an account yet, you can create one when you click Connect to LangRelay under Settings > LangRelay.

How much does it cost?

See langrelay.com/pricing for current plans and prices.

Will this slow down my site?

Not on a typical page view. Approved translations are cached on your site and applied as each page is served, in well under a millisecond on a typical page. About once a minute (the refresh interval), one page view also checks LangRelay for newly activated translations. That check is capped by the API timeout under Settings > LangRelay > Advanced; if LangRelay doesn’t answer in time, the page is served with the translation already cached on your site, or in its original language if it has none yet. Pages also load one small script, deferred so it never holds up the page: every page while your Site counts page views, otherwise pages with the language switcher, translated pages and, while Visitor language is on, every page that has a translation.

Does it handle hreflang tags?

Yes, automatically. On every page with an activated translation, LangRelay adds an hreflang tag for each language version plus an x-default tag pointing to the original. A translated page’s canonical tag names its own address in that language, or, when your SEO plugin points the page at another page of your site, that page’s address in the same language once it is live. No manual SEO work required.

Are my translated pages in a sitemap?

Yes. When your site uses Yoast SEO, Rank Math, All in One SEO, SEOPress, The SEO Framework or XML Sitemap Generator for Google, its sitemap lists each page’s address in every language the page is live in, right after the page itself, and names all of its language versions. A page the SEO plugin leaves out of its sitemap, such as one set to noindex, brings no translated address with it.

When your site uses WordPress’s own sitemap, or no sitemap plugin, LangRelay serves a sitemap at /langrelay-sitemap.xml that lists each page with a live translation and its address in every language it is live in, naming all of its language versions. The robots.txt WordPress writes lists it, and so does WordPress’s own sitemap when your site uses it. LangRelay does the same when the sitemap of one of those plugins is switched off, or the plugin is too old to list translated pages (Yoast SEO before 22.1, Rank Math before 1.0.216, All in One SEO before 4.9.0, SEOPress before 7.0, The SEO Framework before 5.0.6, XML Sitemap Generator for Google before 4.1.20).

A page is listed once its translation is live, never before. LangRelay’s own sitemap lists nothing while your site asks search engines not to index it. If your site has a robots.txt file of its own, Settings → LangRelay shows the line to add to it. A sitemap made by any other plugin does not list your translated pages; LangRelay’s own sitemap does, as above.

Does it work with WooCommerce?

Product and shop pages are translated like any other page once their translation is live. Text that appears after the page loads, such as the mini-cart or an “added to cart” notice, is translated in the visitor’s browser when the same text has an approved translation elsewhere on your site. Parts of a page that change for every visitor, such as a cart’s contents or a checkout’s form fields, can stay in the original language.

Does it work with Yoast SEO and Rank Math?

LangRelay translates the meta titles, meta descriptions, Open Graph and Twitter Card text in your pages’ HTML, whichever plugin writes them — including Yoast SEO and Rank Math — once the page’s translation is live. On a translated page, the canonical, og:url, og:locale and twitter:url they write name the translated page, and their sitemaps list your translated pages (see above).

How do I add the language switcher?

Pick whichever suits your theme:

  • Floating switcher. On by default. Under Settings > LangRelay > Language Switcher, choose the corner it sits in, or switch it off. Pages where you have placed a switcher or a Languages menu item yourself don’t get it.
  • Menus. In Appearance > Menus, add the Languages item to a menu. The languages show as your theme’s own menu items, either the current language with the others below it or side by side.
  • Navigation block. In a block theme, add the Languages block inside your Navigation block.
  • Block editor. Add the Language Switcher block, for example to your header template part.
  • Elementor. Drag in the Language Switcher widget.
  • Shortcode. [langrelay_switcher] works anywhere shortcodes do. Add show_flags="false", show_name="false" or use_native_name="false" to change what each language shows.
  • HTML. Paste <div data-langrelay-switcher></div> into any HTML block or widget. It takes the same options as attributes, like data-show-flags="false".

The switcher’s look is set in the LangRelay Dashboard: one of four styles (Classic, Modern, Commerce or Text), light or dark, a dropdown or a list, and how each language is named. The block, the Elementor widget and the shortcode can give one switcher its own style, layout or label, like [langrelay_switcher style="text" layout="list" label="code"]. Menu items always take your theme’s look.

Can visitors see my site in their own language automatically?

Yes. Your Site’s Visitor language setting, under Settings → WordPress in the LangRelay Dashboard, decides what a visitor who reads another of your languages sees when they arrive:

  • Suggest (the default). A short dialog in the middle of the page offers the page in their language, in that language, with a button to stay in the page’s own language. Nothing changes until they choose, and closing it keeps the page as it is.
  • Redirect. A visitor who arrives from another website is taken to the page in their language before it shows, and told so, with a link back. Search engines advise against automatic redirects, so it is your choice to make.
  • Off. Visitors see the page they asked for.

It only offers a language the page is actually translated into, and only on the first page of a visit. The script that ships with this plugin compares the visitor’s browser languages with the languages each page is translated into; the file that shows the suggestion is served from your site, and nothing is sent to LangRelay or anyone else for this. It never runs for search engines, which are never redirected or shown the suggestion, or for people signed in who can edit posts, so you won’t see it while signed in as someone who can. Settings > LangRelay > Language Switcher shows the current setting. To turn it off, set Visitor language to Off under your Site’s Settings → WordPress in the LangRelay Dashboard.

Visitor language and the language switcher store, in the visitor’s browser only and with no cookie:

  • localStorage["langrelay:language"]: the language the visitor chose, with the date, written only when they click a choice in the suggestion, the notice after a redirect or the language switcher. Deleted after one year.
  • sessionStorage["langrelay:redirected"]: the language of the page an automatic redirect left, written just before the redirect and deleted by the next page as it opens.

Neither ever leaves the visitor’s device.

Does LangRelay show its name on my site?

Yes, by default: a small “Powered by LangRelay” line in the language switcher’s menu and at the bottom of the language suggestion, linking to langrelay.com. On a paid plan you can turn it off, and on again, in the LangRelay Dashboard under your Site’s Appearance settings. On the Free plan it stays on.

What happens if the LangRelay API goes down?

Your site keeps serving the translations it has cached. A page it has no translation for is served in its original language. Nothing breaks.

What is GEO?

GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization. It’s the practice of making your site visible and citable by AI-powered search engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews. LangRelay helps by serving each translation as a real page at its own address, with hreflang tags, so AI search engines can find and cite it in each language.
sections.changelog:
2.22.0

  • New: LangRelay now installs WordPress’s, WooCommerce’s and your theme’s official translations for your languages on its own, at most once a day per language, so your cart and checkout read in your visitors’ language. Turn it off under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced; translations already installed stay.

2.21.3

  • Fix: a search, a sorted or filtered list, or a product option chosen on a translated page no longer makes LangRelay think that page has stopped showing its translation.

2.21.2

  • Improvement: the plugin’s description on WordPress.org is shorter and easier to read, and no longer gets cut off.

2.21.1

  • Improvement: on themes whose headings and paragraphs carry long lists of classes, a title or paragraph that moved on the page is now also shown in the translation your page already has. LangRelay turns this on site by site.
  • New: on your translated pages, a short text that has moved, such as a product card’s title, badge or button shown in a different order, now shows the translation you approved for the same words elsewhere on your site, instead of your site’s own language. LangRelay turns this on site by site, so nothing changes on your site until it does.
  • New: your store’s cart, checkout and account pages can be translated even where your robots.txt asks search engines to skip them. They stay out of search results in every language. Sites that connect from now on get this by default and can turn it off in LangRelay with “Translate my cart, checkout and account pages”. For a site that is already connected, LangRelay turns it on site by site.
  • Fix: on a page with many product cards that shows WordPress’s own translations, texts below the cards, such as the page numbers, now show their translation too.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, a product card’s title or category that follows a button WordPress translated now shows its translation, instead of your site’s own language.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, a sentence your theme and WordPress word slightly differently, such as a product’s “Be the first to review” heading on a store with a theme that has its own “Cancel Reply”, is now recognized and translated, so the page no longer stays in your site’s own language for it.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, star ratings and review counts are no longer counted as missing translations, and the page’s breadcrumb links for search engines now point to the translated pages.
  • Improvement: on a site whose own language is not English (United States), a page that WordPress’s own translations would leave less translated now shows as it did without them. Your cart, checkout and account pages always keep WordPress’s own translations.
  • Improvement: when a page stops using WordPress’s own translations because they left it less translated, LangRelay now notes which of its translated places fell short, so the cause can be found and fixed.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, a form label with an asterisk, such as “Name*” in the comment form, and the last crumb of a breadcrumb now count as translated.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, texts that mix WordPress’s words with your own, such as a page title, a menu’s label, a review’s “verified owner” or your theme’s footer, now show their translation instead of counting as missing. A number that changed since, such as a product count or the year, keeps its current value.
  • Fix: Settings → LangRelay → Advanced now says “On” when “Use WordPress’s own translations” is on, instead of describing it as off.
  • Fix: on pages that show WordPress’s own translations, your product and tag names inside WordPress’s sentences, such as “Be the first to review” or a product’s quantity label, now show their translation instead of staying in your site’s own language.
  • Fix: on product tag pages that show WordPress’s own translations, the breadcrumb links for search engines now point to the translated page.

2.21.0

  • New: LangRelay’s Overview now tells you when WordPress’s own translations for one of your languages are missing, and installs them in one click. These translations cover the buttons, form fields and totals that WordPress, WooCommerce and your theme write on your cart, checkout and account pages. Without them, some of those words stay in your site’s language. The button uses WordPress’s own installer, which downloads the translations from WordPress.org. Nothing is installed until someone who may install languages clicks it.
  • Improvement: when a page’s translation changes, your page cache now shows the new translation within a minute or two instead of when the cache expires. This works with W3 Total Cache, WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, WP Super Cache, WP Fastest Cache, Cache Enabler, SiteGround Optimizer, Nginx Helper, Breeze and SpinupWP. A server cache with none of these plugins still refreshes when it expires.
  • New: WordPress’s own translations now work on sites whose own language is not US English. WooCommerce, your theme, your plugins and WordPress itself show their official translations on your translated pages, cart and checkout included. Any text they have no translation for keeps LangRelay’s translation, as before. LangRelay turns this on site by site, so nothing changes on your site until it does. On an English page with no British or other English translation installed, WordPress’s US English is used. If you prefer LangRelay’s wording for a plugin, switch that plugin off under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced.
  • Fix: a shopper who buys in a translated language now stays in that language. Adding to cart from a translated product page, the cart, the checkout and the order confirmation keep the language’s address, and the order confirmation, the order payment page and My account’s pages no longer show “page not found” there. Paginated lists under a translated address work too.
  • Fix: on a store in US English with WooCommerce’s classic checkout and WordPress’s translations installed for a language, the translated checkout was shown in English as soon as the cart held a product. The translated country list puts countries in a new order, and the names that are spelled the same in both languages were counted as missing. The checkout is now shown translated. This needs WordPress 6.5 or later.
  • Fix: the first-page checklist in Settings → LangRelay no longer says your page is live before it is. Until LangRelay has verified the translated page live, its heading reads “Get your homepage live in …”, and then “Your homepage is live in …”.
  • Fix: on a site with WordPress’s own language packs installed, translated pages no longer fall back to the original language because the packs translated a date, a button, a label or a theme’s footer text. Text of your own next to it, such as a product name, still gets its LangRelay translation.
  • Fix: a page whose list of products or posts changed order, and that shows one of those items again further down, is no longer shown in its original language because of it.
  • Fix: in the moment after your first page goes live, visitors see the plain list of languages where your language switcher is placed, instead of no switcher at all, until the switcher is ready.
  • Improvement: switching language keeps your place on the page. A visitor who opens a link like /#about or /?utm_source=ad#pricing and picks another language lands on the same section of the translated page, with the same campaign parameters, instead of at the top.
  • Fix: text a translation keeps exactly as written, such as a price, a product name or a “Home” link, no longer counts towards how much of a page is translated. A page with too much text still in its original language is shown in that language, as intended.
  • Fix: a section that shows different items on every visit, such as a “You may also like” list of products, no longer counts towards how much of a page is translated. Such a page is no longer shown in its original language just because that section changed.

2.20.0

short_description: Make your site multilingual with AI translation, live as you choose. Automatic hreflang, canonical tags, SEO metadata and a language switcher.
description:
LangRelay is a WordPress translation plugin that makes your site multilingual. AI translates your pages, posts and products. Each translation goes live as you choose in the LangRelay Dashboard, and your site serves it at its own address, with hreflang tags and a language switcher handled automatically.

Most translation plugins stop at the words on the page. LangRelay also translates your meta titles and descriptions and gives every translated page its own address, so your site gets found in every market you sell in.

What you get

  • AI translations, live as you choose. Machine translation drafts each page; it goes live once ready (the default), after a hold, or only once you approve it. Free checks hold a page with untranslated text, the wrong language or a changed price; legal pages, pricing pages and sweeping changes always wait for you.
  • An address for every language. Each translated page lives under its language prefix, like yoursite.com/nl/about-us, and you can give it an address in that language, like yoursite.com/nl/over-ons, in the LangRelay Dashboard.
  • Automatic hreflang and SEO metadata. Hreflang and canonical tags on every translated page with no manual setup, and translated meta titles, descriptions and social text (details below).
  • Language switcher. A menu or list with flags and language names, in one of four styles. A plain list of links is rendered with the page, so visitors without JavaScript and search engines still see every language. Add it as a Gutenberg block, Elementor widget, shortcode, HTML snippet or menu items, or float it in the corner you choose.
  • WooCommerce pages. Product and shop pages translate like any other page once their translation is live.
  • Visitors offered their language. A visitor who reads one of your languages is offered the page in it or, if you choose, taken there on arrival. Set it in the LangRelay Dashboard.

Why a multilingual WordPress site matters

  • English is only 16% of the internet. The other 84% is your addressable market.
  • Google ranks translated pages separately. A multilingual site can multiply your organic traffic without adding new content.
  • AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini) increasingly answer in the user’s native language. Without translated pages, you don’t show up.

How it works

  1. Install the plugin, go to Settings > LangRelay and click Connect to LangRelay. Sign in to LangRelay or create your account there, approve the connection in the LangRelay Dashboard, and you’re back on your site, connected.
  2. In the LangRelay Dashboard, pick your languages.
  3. Approve your first page there; after it, pages follow your setting. Once a translation is live, your site serves it at its own address, with the language switcher, hreflang and canonical tags taken care of.

No content duplication, no manual translation interface, no separate posts to manage.

Multilingual SEO done right

LangRelay handles the SEO work that usually takes hours per language:

  • hreflang and x-default tags on every translated page and its original
  • A canonical tag on every translated page naming its own address in that language. When your SEO plugin points a page’s canonical at another page of your site, the translation points at that page in the same language once it is live; a canonical to another website is left as it is
  • An address of its own for each language version, under its language prefix, with the page’s lang (and dir="rtl" for a right-to-left language)
  • Translated meta titles, descriptions, and Open Graph and Twitter text in your page’s HTML, whichever plugin writes them
  • og:url, og:locale, an og:locale:alternate for each other language the page is live in, and twitter:url, naming the translated page’s own address and language
  • Your translated pages in the sitemaps of Yoast SEO, Rank Math, All in One SEO, SEOPress, The SEO Framework and XML Sitemap Generator for Google, each with all its language versions
  • A sitemap of your translated pages when your site uses WordPress’s own sitemap or no sitemap plugin

Search engines understand which language to serve to which visitor.

What makes LangRelay different

Your site serves exactly the translation LangRelay recorded as live.

The same sentence is translated once and reused wherever it appears, even on 500 pages, like a line in your footer.

Pricing

Plans and prices are at langrelay.com/pricing.

Meet Relay

Relay is the AI assistant in the LangRelay Dashboard. Ask it about your Site, and it can start machine translation for a page, fetch a page again after you change it, or suggest a better translation for a sentence you select. It never approves a translation itself.

External services

LangRelay’s Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Data Processing Agreement are at langrelay.com. By using this plugin you agree to LangRelay’s Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

LangRelay API, from your site

Your site calls the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) over HTTPS, always with this site’s connection credential. It never sends your page content.

What is sent: when you connect, the one-time connection code. On connecting and in an hourly health check: your site’s address, WordPress and plugin versions and an installation ID. The health check also says whether WooCommerce is installed and active, and its version and, while it is active, the addresses of your store’s published cart, checkout and account pages; which of Yoast SEO, Rank Math, All in One SEO, SEOPress, The SEO Framework or XML Sitemap Generator for Google makes your sitemap, and its version (or that WordPress’s own sitemap, or none, does); and whether your site has its own robots.txt. No other plugin is named. About a minute after you save content: the address of each published page you saved, or that a menu, category, tag, site title, tagline or theme changed, with the time and installation ID. Within ten minutes of an update to WordPress, an active plugin or your theme: its name and old and new versions. Within ten minutes of a translated page being shown in its original language because your page layout changed (each page at most once every six hours): which page and language, and how much of the translation still fitted. When you erase a customer’s personal data: their profile key (see revenue below), again later if LangRelay could not be reached.
What is received: your site’s languages and your pages’ approved translations, which the plugin caches on your site. It checks them hourly with the health check, and on visitor page requests at most once per refresh interval (one minute by default) or when an approved translation changes. Only when an administrator opens Settings > LangRelay, at most every five minutes (or a minute later when LangRelay could not be reached): your LangRelay plan, this month’s word usage and welcome grant, the pages waiting to be translated (titles and addresses) and the plan that would translate them now, with its price and a link to the LangRelay Dashboard. Only while that screen is open and in view, at most every half minute (it asks every twenty seconds and stops after twenty minutes; a minute later when LangRelay could not be reached): how far your first translation has come (the language, how many texts are translated, whether the page is live and checked), the live page’s address and a link to your Site in the LangRelay Dashboard.

LangRelay API, from your visitors’ browsers

A small script that ships with this plugin, served from your site and never from LangRelay, calls the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) from the visitor’s browser: on every page while your Site counts page views; otherwise on pages with the language switcher, on translated pages and, while Visitor language is on, on every page that has a translation. It follows your Site’s Dynamic content setting in LangRelay, on by default.

Translations: when a visitor opens a page, unless their browser has a fresh copy, it reads your site’s languages and, on a translated page, the approved, live translations in that language it needs for text that appears after the page loads (such as a mini-cart) and the addresses of your translated pages. It sends your site’s public key (printed in the page, not a password) and, on a translated page, its language and which part of your translations it needs (a version and a part number).
Page views, for your Site’s visitor analytics: once for each page a visitor opens, it sends your site’s public key; the page’s address without any query string; the visitor’s language as your site names it; whether the page was shown translated, could have been, or was read in the original language; and, when another website’s link brought the visitor, that website’s domain name only. Never the page’s text or title, any cookie, the full address of the page the visitor came from, or any identifier, except the profile key of a customer signed in to your shop while revenue tracking is on. Nothing is received. From it LangRelay works out the visitor’s country, kind of device, browser and operating system, and a visitor code that changes every day, so a visitor cannot be recognised from one day to the next (a signed-in customer’s profile key is the one exception); the IP address and browser details are used only for that and never stored. Counting stores nothing on the visitor’s device. Page views are kept for three months, then only totals. None is sent when the browser has Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track on, or for people signed in with a role left out under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced (administrators and editors by default). Counting is on by default: switch off Visitor analytics under your Site’s Settings → Analytics in the LangRelay Dashboard, and it stops within about a minute. LangRelay’s Privacy Policy and Data Processing Agreement describe how this data is handled.

Visitor language, in your visitors’ browsers

Suggesting or redirecting to a visitor’s language sends nothing to anyone. It stores the visitor’s choice and a redirect marker in their browser (localStorage, sessionStorage, no cookie; details in the FAQ).

WordPress’s own translations, from WordPress.org

Translated pages use the official translations of WordPress, your theme and plugins installed on your site. Once a day at most per language, WordPress’s own installer downloads those of WordPress, WooCommerce and your theme that a language lacks (on your click, your plugins’ too), from WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org, downloads.wordpress.org); turn this off under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced. It sends what WordPress sends when it checks for updates: your WordPress version, your site’s languages and the versions of your active plugins and theme. Nothing goes to LangRelay. The WordPress.org Privacy Policy applies.

The “Powered by LangRelay” link

The language switcher’s menu and the language suggestion show a “Powered by LangRelay” link to langrelay.com, on by default (a paid plan can turn it off in the LangRelay Dashboard). Only when a visitor clicks it does langrelay.com open in a new tab, with your site’s domain name, whether the link was in the switcher or the suggestion, and your site’s public key in its address, so LangRelay can tell which site the visit came from. The page the visitor was on is not sent.

LangRelay API, for your shop’s revenue (WooCommerce)

When WooCommerce is active and you switch on revenue tracking (off by default) under your Site’s Settings → Analytics in the LangRelay Dashboard, your site’s server, never the shopper’s browser, tells the LangRelay API (api.langrelay.com) what happens to its orders, so the Dashboard can show your revenue and the language each order came from. Nothing is sent while it is off.

What is sent, about a minute after an order is placed at checkout, paid, refunded or cancelled, in batches and again later if LangRelay could not be reached: the order’s ID, what happened, the amount (the order’s total, or the refund’s) with its currency, when it happened, and the language the shopper browsed in (the checkout page’s, or else that of the page they last added a product from, which WooCommerce keeps in the shopper’s existing cart session; no new cookie); a signed-in customer’s profile key (below); this site’s connection credential and installation ID. For an order placed at checkout, also the shopper’s IP address and browser details as WooCommerce recorded them, which LangRelay turns into that day’s visitor code and never stores. Never the shopper’s name, email address, postal address, phone number, customer account or what they bought. What is received: whether each order event was recorded. Orders are kept while your Site exists; an order’s visitor code is removed 90 days after the order. Switching revenue tracking off stops the sending within about a minute and drops what was not sent yet.

Customers signed in to your shop: while revenue tracking is on, each gets a pseudonymous profile key, so the Dashboard can show which pages your customers came in on before they ordered. Your site’s server computes it from their account number in your shop and a secret LangRelay hands it, never from an email address, and it does not name them. It is printed in the pages they view, sent with their page views and orders, and links their visits across days. Never for guests, for people signed in with a role left out under Settings → LangRelay → Advanced, or, when the WP Consent API plugin is installed, for a visitor who has not consented to statistics. LangRelay keeps it on page views for three months and on orders for as long as the order. When you erase a customer’s personal data under Tools > Erase Personal Data, the plugin asks LangRelay to remove their key from their orders and never computes one for them again. LangRelay receives no name, email address or customer number with it.

LangRelay Dashboard

Only when you click Connect to LangRelay does your browser go to the LangRelay Dashboard (app.langrelay.com) to approve the connection and back, with your site’s address, installation ID, WordPress site language, title (which names your LangRelay organization) and the address to return to in the address your browser opens.

Only when you click Upgrade in the Dashboard on Settings > LangRelay does the LangRelay Dashboard’s plan page open in a new tab, at the address LangRelay gave, with your organization’s ID and the suggested plan in that address. The plugin never changes your plan; you upgrade in the Dashboard.
